title: Imaging Synaptic Decline in Models of Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by a failure in synapses and
consequently the progressive deterioration of cognitive functions. The amyloid β peptide (Aβ) and APOE
genotype are critical initiators that trigger the progression of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) I propose an optical
imaging approach to investigate the loss of synaptic function associated with Aβ and APOE genotype contribute
to the physiological consequences of aging and AD.

title: A Hydro-Meteorological Malaria Model for Adaptive and Tailored Vector Control Strategies in Africa
text:
This project will develop a novel tool that integrates weather, environmental, and entomological
data to enhance the prediction of where and when malaria outbreaks are likely to occur. It will
also improve understanding of how environmental changes and mosquito ecology influence
malaria transmission risk. The tool will support the design of effective vector control strategies
informed by environmental and ecological conditions.

title: Multi-omic liquid biopsy assessment in NCI trials: evaluating ctDNA, extravesicle RNA, and outcomes with immunotherapy in patient with colorectal and anal cancers
text:
As a clinical scientist, I have led (as overall Principal Investigator) first-in-kind NCI-supported clinical trials
evaluating circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) as a predictive biomarker for adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with
early-stage colon cancer as well as trials testing novel immunotherapy combinations for patients with incurable
gastrointestinal malignancies. My research interest focuses on use of the liquid biopsy to characterize genomic
(ctDNA) and transcriptomic (extravesicle RNA) changes in association with treatment responses, using
plasma samples that may overcome historical challenges of obtaining paired tumor biopsy samples from
clinical trials. In seeking R50 funding, I propose to apply these learned experiences to develop other NCI-led
clinical trials for colorectal cancer and anal cancer that, if successful, would validate the use of the liquid biopsy
as tool valuable for the design of clinical trials aimed to eradicate minimal residual disease (as informed by a
“ctDNA(+) status”) and improve survival outcomes for patients with gastrointestinal malignancies.

title: Predicting trajectories of function, cognition, and quality of life among older adults with advanced lung cancer
text:
Over 71% of patients with newly diagnosed lung cancer are aged >65 and more than 50% are diagnosed with
advanced disease, resulting in a large growing population of older adults with advanced non-small cell lung
cancer (NSCLC). This project will provide oncologists with pragmatic clinical tools developed with
generalizable data to predict individualized trajectories for function, cognition, and quality of life for older adults
with advanced NSCLC during chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy treatment. This project supports the
National Institute on Aging’s goal to promote the health and well-being of older adults and to mitigate the
impact of aging-related conditions.

title: eDyNAmiC - NYU
text: eDyNAmiC (extrachromosomal DNA in Cancer) Human genes are arranged on 23 pairs of chromosomes, but in cancer, tumour-promoting genes can free themselves from chromosomes and relocate to circular, extrachromosomal pieces of DNA (ecDNA). These ecDNA do not follow the normal “rules” of chromosomal inheritance, enabling tumours to achieve far higher levels of cancer-causing oncogenes than would otherwise be possible, and licensing cancers with a way to evolve and change their genomes to evade treatments at rates that would be unthinkable for human cells. The altered circular architecture of ecDNAs also changes the way that the cancer-causing genes are regulated and expressed, further contributing to aggressive tumour growth. These unique features make ecDNA-containing cancers especially aggressive and difficult to treat. Cancer patients whose tumours harbour ecDNA have markedly shorter survival. Despite being first seen over fifty years ago, the critical importance of ecDNA has only recently come to light, and the scale of the problem is substantial. ecDNAs are present in nearly half of all human cancer types and potentially up-to a third of all cancer patients. The collective current understanding of how ecDNA form, how they function, how they move around the cell, how they evolve to resist treatment, how they impact the immune system, and how they can be effectively targeted are lacking. We bring together an internationally recognized, pioneering interdisciplinary team of cancer biologists, geneticists, computer scientists, evolutionary biologists, mathematicians, clinicians, and patient advocates to boldly create novel insights and resources and to provide transformative solutions to one of Cancer’s Grand Challenges. A core team of experienced and productive ecDNA investigators will work with new investigators in the ecDNA and cancer fields to bring completely new perspectives and approaches to this daunting challenge. By bridging cutting-edge and diverse approaches and insights from cancer genomics, yeast genetics, epigenomics, artificial genome synthesis, longitudinal patient tracking, combinatorial and machine learning algorithms, mathematical modelling, immunobiology, and innovative chemistry we will develop a new understanding of the role of ecDNA in cancer, and we will find new ways to drug the undruggable. This bold programme, which consists of 7 work packages and a committed international infrastructure, generates new and unusual collaborations that would simply be impossible under any other type of funding mechanism. Our programme endeavours to foster bold innovative solutions to one of the hardest problems in cancer and to one of the greatest challenges facing cancer patients.

title: Mechanisms of persistent neural activity
text:
The proposed work aims to understand the cellular and circuit contributions to persistent neural activity,
thought to be the neural basis of working memory and a building block of many forms of cognition. Deﬁcits in
these functions are evident in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimers, schizophrenia, and a number of other brain
diseases. Being able to repair or replace the mechanisms of persistent activity would be of signiﬁcant clinical
relevance to this large set of human health challenges.

title: A geospatial analysis of hotspots and targeted injection settings pilot intervention for HIV prevention among people who inject drugs in Baltimore, Maryland
text:
Relevance
PWID continue to have high rates of HIV and high mortality rates in the US. The proposed methods have the potential to rapidly identify hotspots without major HIV testing initiatives and can help health departments target HIV prevention and care efforts. The proposed intervention will cover a large geographic area and enhance access to HIV prevention and drug treatment materials, peer education, and naloxone.

title: Membrane protein-mediated signaling as a driver of spermiogenesis- Investigating new molecules and mechanisms
text:
Millions of round spermatids within the testis must undergo a remarkable morphological change to form motile
sperm capable of fertilizing an egg, but the molecules and mechanisms that drive this critical process are poorly
understood. We have identified a new protein, TMC5, that is required to drive spermatid elongation, and whose
absence results in azoospermia- the complete lack of sperm. Here, we will use novel mouse models and cutting-
edge imaging technology to elucidate the specific role of TMC5 in sperm development, thus enhancing our
understanding of causes of male infertility.

title: Molecular mechanisms of gating and selectivity in the MscS and MRS2 superfamilies of channels
text:
Mechanosensitive channels participate in an array of fundamental physiological processes, including hearing,
touch, proprioception, osmoregulation, and morphogenesis. Magnesium homeostasis is pivotal for many
cellular functions, and abnormal magnesium levels cause various metabolic diseases including obesity,
diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Our proposed structural and functional studies of mechanosensitive and
magnesium channels will provide critical information that will ultimately lead to development of new treatment
strategies for diseases associated with altered mechanical force sensation or dysregulated magnesium levels.

title: REGULATORS OF EPIDERMAL GENE EXPRESSION
text:
REGULATORS OF EPIDERMAL GENE EXPRESSION
 Project Narrative
Self-renewing tissues, like the cutaneous epidermis, require a balance between proliferation
and differentiation to maintain human health. This balance is disrupted in common human skin
diseases. This project characterizes new regulators that control this process with a goal to
enable future applications in biomedicine.

title: High performance miniaturized microscopes for through skull cortex-wide imaging in freely behaving mice
text:
In this proposal, Objective Biotechnology seeks to develop a commercial-grade miniaturized fluorescence
microscope with a high sensitivity CMOS that can perform wide-field calcium imaging through an intact skull.
Successful accomplishment of this project will result in a new robust tool for use in pre-clinical neuroscience
studies of large scale neural dynamics.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of V-ATPases: Assembly, Biogenesis, Regulation, and Function
text:
The vacuolar ATPases (V-ATPases) are large, multi-subunit proton pumps that are essential for many
fundamental physiological processes in all eukaryotic organisms and malfunction of V-ATPases is
associated with devastating human diseases including cancer, renal tubular acidosis, osteoporosis,
diabetes, neurodegenerative diseases, and AIDS. Elucidating the structures and molecular
mechanisms of V-ATPases assembly, biogenesis, regulation, and signaling will greatly advance our
understanding of these V-ATPase-associated diseases. The completion of the project will not only
advance our understanding on V-ATPases but also offer mechanistic insights to modulate human V-
ATPase activity for disease treatment.

title: Restoring HLA-I Expression to Enhance CD8 T Cell-Mediated Clearance of HIV-Infected Cells
text:
HIV persists despite antiretroviral therapy (ART) due to latent reservoirs that evade immune detection. This
project will determine whether IL-15, in combination with PTPN1/2 inhibition, rescues HLA-I expression on HIV-
infected cells and enhances recognition and killing by CD8 T cells, and why certain viral subtypes resist this
effect. Findings will inform strategies to optimize immunotherapies that improve CD8 T cell–mediated
clearance of HIV reservoirs and advance cure-focused approaches.

title: Role of disparities and aging biomarkers in accelerated cardiac aging among adolescent and young adult cancer survivors
text: Survivors of adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer are likely to live several more decades, yet their previous treatment exposures can have dramatic long-term effects on their cardiovascular health. Our preliminary research suggests that there is a group of survivors of AYA cancer whose hearts are functioning at the same levels as hearts in individuals who are decades older. We have initiated the development of a survivor of AYA cancer study designed to identify the characteristics of accelerated cardiac aging that can inform strategies reduce risk during treatment and develop personalized risk-informed follow-up care to reduce and prevent the development of cardiac dysfunction.

title: The Ohio State University Vision Sciences Research Core Program (OSU-VSRCP)
text:
NARRATIVE for P30
The purpose of The Ohio State University Vision Sciences Research Core Program (OSU-VSRCP) is to
enhance the environment for NEI-funded PIs and other vision science faculty who represent five Colleges:
Medicine, Optometry, Veterinary Medicine, Engineering and Arts & Sciences. Three cores are proposed based
on a survey of 61 scientists: Core A-Structural and Functional Assessments, Core B-Biostatistics,
Bioinformatics and Genetic Analysis, and Core C-Image Analysis and Data Science. The institutional
commitment (i.e., support the Program Director includes successful recruitment of vision scientists, space for a
new confocal microscope purchase for Core A, and space in the 2023 Interdisciplinary Research Facility)
supports our common goal to prevent blindness, restore vision and develop cures for eye diseases.

title: Bacteriophage diversity, dynamics, function, and exploitation
text:
Bacteriophages are the most numerous organisms in the biosphere and profoundly influence
microbial diversity, bacterial pathogenesis, and biotechnological advances. Dynamic
bacteriophage-bacterium interactions contribute to narrow patterns of host specificity by phages,
driven by bacterially encoded defense systems, prophage-mediated defense systems, and
plasmids. Elucidating these systems and their roles in phage host range will advance our
understanding of microbial dynamics and fuel the development of phage-based therapeutics.

title: CORE B: Omics Core
text: (DHART SPORE OMICS CORE, CORE B) The Developmental and HyperActive Ras Tumor (DHART) SPORE was designed to integrate multiple research projects, all with the goal of identifying novel molecular therapeutic strategies for NF1-related malignancies. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder, characterized by mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin. Functional loss of neurofibromin, a Ras-GTPase activating protein (GAP) leads to hyperactive Ras signaling and dysregulation of multiple cell signaling pathways impacting cell proliferation and survival, such as Raf-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR. Analysis of baseline models, patient heterogeneity, and intrinsic and adaptive responses to Project-defined therapeutic strategies will be performed. The overall goal of the DHART SPORE Omics Core (Core B) is to provide state-of-the-art support for research design consultation, execution of genomics and kinomics experiments, and integrated data analysis to DHART SPORE investigators. Built upon institutional genomics cores (Center for Medical Genomics), an established kinome/proteomics laboratory, and a bioinformatics research center (Center for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics), Core B also interacts intensively with other cores for supporting the DHART investigators. Upon receipt of tracked samples from the DHART SPORE Biospecimen and Pathology Core (Core C), the following technologies and informatics platforms will be employed by Core B: 1) Bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing, whole exome sequencing, targeted exome sequencing, methyl-ome sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics. 2) Analysis and annotation of sequencing data for Project investigators and transfer to Synapse, the Sage portal for data analysis. 3) Established and novel proteomics approaches to provide functional, activity-based, kinase network profiles of specimens—defining baseline kinome state, effects of specific genotype or genetic perturbations, and drug target and network response to treatment. 4) Integrative analysis support (in collaboration with DHART SPORE Administrative and Biostatistics Core, Core A, and Sage Bionetworks) to provide comprehensive molecular profiles of genotype-driven gene expression and functional kinase network profiles. The profiles will be studied for both putative response biomarkers and for candidate therapeutic targets. Synapse, a web portal maintained by Sage will allow access by SPORE investigators of all data obtained by Core B and Core C, where findings will be annotated and made more broadly useful to all investigators involved in the SPORE. This data management portal will provide a unique resource for accessing and interpreting data generated by the three projects, Core C and Core B.

title: Readily Available Biological Conduits to Treat Single Ventricle Defects
text:
Existing therapeutic interventions for single ventricle congenital heart defects, including synthetic or tissue-
engineered vascular conduits made by seeding autologous patient bone marrow cells onto biodegradable
polymeric tubular scaffolds, are insufficient for effective patient care due to vulnerability to infection, thrombosis,
inability to grow, or a high incidence of graft stenosis after transplantation. Native blood vessel scaffolds and
human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived endothelial cells, capable of mitigating thrombosis and
cellular over-proliferation during vascular conduit generation, may offer an opportunity to effectively address the
above challenges. This project describes our efforts to develop universal, hypoimmunogenic contractile conduits
based on hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, cardiac fibroblasts, and endothelial cells that can prevent graft stenosis
and provide pumping activity to assist blood flow through both in vitro assays and in vivo implantation into an
immune-humanized rat model.

title: Understanding Infantile Rhabdomyosarcoma Biology and Therapeutic Targets
text:
Infantile rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a newly identified and poorly understood aggressive pediatric muscle
cancer that affects young children. There is one single mutation that causes the disease, but we do not have
specialized treatments targeting this genetic event, and patients are treated with general strategies that are often
ineffective or have harsh life-long side effects. We will leverage novel zebrafish and mouse cancer models to
help young children with cancer by understanding the biology of how infantile RMS develops and implementing
these models to identify clinically tractable therapeutic targets.

title: A genotype-phenotype study of germline succinate dehydrogenase pathogenic variants
text:
Succinate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial complex with critical roles in metabolism and. Inherited loss-of-
function variants in the succinate dehydrogenase genes are causative in several human cancers, and tumors
have been linked to DNA damage. This proposal aims to accurately characterize the phenotypes and tumor
biology associated with succinate dehydrogenase germline pathogenic variants, to develop improved risk
estimates and evaluate potential targeted therapies for patients who progress to disease.
